Replay

Replay transports

7 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Closing transport wrappersDeterministic memory adapterShared packet routingGodot ENet adapterFragmentation and browser WebRTCConnection generationsRecording a real interface

Use Transport to drive packet delivery independently of the simulation and its network policy. It is a borrowed interface over a concrete adapter. It provides send, receive, poll, status, peer_connected, and close. Accepted sends copy payloads; receive copies into caller storage. Buffer_Too_Small retains the pending packet and reports the required size. A peer ID identifies a transport connection, not a stable player seat. Session admission and reconnect identity are separate work.

Packets are bounded to 64 KiB at this interface. A transport may have a smaller configured limit. There is no implicit broadcast: callers explicitly enumerate recipients. Reliable is ordered per direction/channel; Unreliable may lose, duplicate, or reorder messages. Check Backpressure and retry according to the session's delivery policy.

Closing transport wrappers#

A Transport value is a borrowed handle, so copying it never creates another connection owner. Closing a handle invokes its adapter's close callback. Wrapper callbacks have these specific effects:

Wrapper interface Effect of close
delay_transport Closes its base and frees the delay queue.
remap_transport Closes its base and clears the mapping.
fragments_transport Frees fragmentation storage; leaves its base open.
router_transport Closes that lane; leaves the router and base open.

Close a forwarding wrapper as one stack; do not separately close stale copies of its base handle. For a borrowing wrapper, destroy its dependent runners first, close/destroy the wrapper, then close the base adapter. After closing all router lanes, call router_destroy to free the router's buffers, then close its base. These rules also apply when wrappers are composed: closing Fragments over Delay leaves Delay open until its own handle is closed.

Deterministic memory adapter#

Memory owns preallocated packet storage, endpoint registration, RNG, and bounded trace storage. Open distinct Memory_Endpoints, obtain their interfaces with memory_transport, and advance the network with memory_advance. Nothing uses a wall clock. Close endpoints before destroying their network owner.

Faults controls latency/jitter in ticks, loss and duplication per 10,000 packets, and reliable retry delay. Reliable packets remain queued through a 100% loss blackout; unreliable packets drop. Reliable order is preserved even when later packets become ready first. Full queues return backpressure without partial sends.

This models the service contract of reliable/unreliable channels, not ENet's congestion/retransmission algorithm. It does not establish a real-network result. Reproduction requires the initial config/seed, timed fault changes, input/send schedule, and time-advance schedule. The bounded trace and its logical hash help compare runs; trace_dropped explicitly reports incomplete trace retention.

Shell
nix develop --command bash tests/replay_transport/run.sh

Shared packet routing#

Router supplies two borrowed transport views over one connection. Call router_pump once before pumping either consumer. Their Transport.poll callbacks do not poll again, so adding consumers cannot multiply the ingress budget. Bounded packet and byte rings preserve metadata and retain too-small reads. Unreliable overflow drops only that lane's datagram. Reliable overflow retains one pending packet until its lane drains, so reliable delivery is not silently weakened; this can temporarily hold up the underlying queue. The recovery link routes checkpoint messages to its background lane and negotiates their delivery channel as described in the recovery contract.

Both views share a token bucket and per-pump output limit. Background sends also leave primary_reserve bytes available for gameplay. Callers receive backpressure instead of an implicit send queue. router_destroy frees buffers but does not close the underlying owner. Three native tests cover queue isolation, reliable retention, wrapped byte storage, small receives, aggregate output bounds, and reserved capacity.

Godot ENet adapter#

Enet from replay/godot/transport owns a directly polled ENetMultiplayerPeer. It does not install SceneMultiplayer or use Kit. Construct it with enet_host/enet_join, then use enet_transport. enet_id returns the current connection's ID after it connects. Host bind defaults to all interfaces; tests explicitly bind loopback.

The adapter uses channel 0's independent reliable/unreliable transfer modes, as defined by Godot's MultiplayerPeer contract. It owns/releases its peer reference, connection-tracking callables, and pending receive buffer. Connection signals maintain a live peer set without game-script callbacks, so disconnected recipients are rejected before sending. Polling a disconnected peer is a no-op. ENet constructors return false on Godot web targets; a WebRTC adapter is still required.

Delay is a bounded receive-delay decorator for real transports. It preserves delivery order, packet ownership, connection visibility, and backpressure. The Hello network gate uses it to inject 120 ms receive delay on each process.

Shell
nix develop --command bash tests/replay_enet/run.sh

That gate starts a server and two client processes, transfers canonical world envelopes in both delivery modes, verifies sender metadata and decoded data, and requires clean shutdown. It is a transport/codec acceptance test, not the roadmap's server-prediction/client/observer gameplay acceptance gate.

Fresh project preparation uses a normal headless editor startup for 120 frames, allowing queued editor work to finish. The immediate --import shutdown path exhibited a first-scan crash in the existing editor integration; this remains an explicit tooling follow-up, rather than an ignored test failure.

Fragmentation and browser WebRTC#

fragments_init wraps a borrowed transport whose reliable channel preserves packet order. Both ends must use the same MTU. It copies accepted logical messages into bounded queues, fragments up to 64 KiB, expires partial unreliable assemblies, and retains reliable data through receiver backpressure. The live peer count must fit Fragment_Config.messages, which also bounds delivery-frontier tracking. Closing this wrapper does not close its borrowed base.

The Godot RTC adapter composes fragmentation with raw negotiated data channels and receiver credit. This additional credit prevents Godot's finite JS ring from dropping already SCTP-delivered reliable data. rtc_transport is a normal Replay interface; Session_Options.backend = .Rtc uses it through the same server/client gameplay runner. Browser migration has separate Room acceptance; public relay/TURN deployment still needs its own acceptance.

Fragment transmission selects queued messages by acceptance order and skips a blocked peer/channel for the current poll. Reused array slots do not determine send order or prevent the sender from using its remaining packet budget. The sustained-small-message regression covers queue wrap; reliable ordering and receiver backpressure tests remain separate checks.

Connection generations#

Transport.generation is an optional callback exposed through peer_generation. A versioned adapter supplies a nonzero generation for each connection and changes it when a numeric peer ID is rebound within the same open transport lifetime. Received.generation carries that local metadata for received/retained packets; it is not read from a gameplay payload and does not authenticate a member. Closing an owner ends its borrowed handles. Generations are not persisted across a closed transport owner or serialized in packets/checkpoints.

Memory increments the generation when an endpoint ID reopens. WebRTC uses its peer-connection serial, including explicit replacement of creator ID 1. Healthy signaling continuation preserves the serial. Delay, Router, Fragments and Remap propagate the callback and packet metadata. Delayed and routed packets from a retired generation are discarded; fragment assemblies, pending input, queued output and delivery frontiers are retired separately for that connection. The wrappers expose retired counters in their existing diagnostics.

Custom wrappers must forward the callback to retain these guarantees. An adapter without it remains unversioned (generation == 0); receive normalizes its metadata accordingly, preserving the old interface behavior. Such an adapter must still fence old traffic when reusing IDs, or construct a new wrapper/transport owner. This feature does not add reliable delivery across a disconnected session; the enclosing protocol decides what may be retransmitted or recovered.

The transport suite checks ID reuse with delayed/queued/pending reliable packets, partial and completed fragments, reused message IDs, outbound queues, delivery frontiers, independent peers and unversioned-wrapper compatibility. The creator-recovery browser gate keeps a live P2P runner while the authenticated creator returns at ID 1 with a new connection generation.

fragments_limit_unreliable optionally bounds staged unreliable datagrams per recipient. Set it while the transmit queue is empty; zero leaves the ordinary message/byte limits alone. One large logical packet remains admissible when that recipient's unreliable queue is empty, even if it exceeds the pacing bound by itself. Further messages wait for capacity. Reliable messages retain their existing ordering and admission, and global memory/message limits remain in force.

RTC uses a bound of eight staged unreliable datagrams in addition to its existing 16-packet credit window. This applies backpressure before several stale snapshots accumulate inside the adapter. It does not drop accepted packets, change wire framing, enlarge receive buffers or prioritize away checkpoint traffic. Fragment_Stats.queue_limited records those admission deferrals.

Recording a real interface#

The optional trace package captures exact transport callback observations with bounded owned storage and preserves nil-callback semantics. Strict playback checks caller operations and outbound bytes without opening a real endpoint. Caller marks can record pump times/configuration; the Claimball observer fixture also compares per-frame state and effect hashes.
